blocks.text: Job 26 belongs to the sustained debate that follows the friends’ initial seven days of silence. Job had already cursed the day of his birth, while Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar increasingly explained his suffering through wrongdoing—a diagnosis Job rejects. This larger setting helps explain why Job’s opening questions sound sharply critical rather than like neutral instruction.

Later readers have understood Job’s endurance as persistence through suffering and as part of the story’s eventual outcome. That understanding need not turn Job into a model of silent submission to abuse or deny the need for escape and protection; throughout the book, Job speaks, protests, and continues the argument.
